- A new boss
- New Traits

Before i start the actual review I want to point out that Hunt Showdown is an EXTRACTION SHOOTER. These games are very often defined by slow gameplay, high stakes, permadeath and most importantly dying often. If these concepts seem annoying to you and ruin the experience for you, then Hunt will most probably not be your game and dropping a bad review about it being the game that it is doesn’t help that fact.
If you do like those concepts, then the game is in my opinion one of the best Titles in the genre and there are many dopamine hits to be chased.

Now to the more detailed stuff:
I have played around 1100 hours. A few years ago the game was maybe more grounded than before, which in my opinion has pros and cons. I find the event mechanics interesting and they definitely impact the gameplay more than before, but sometimes maybe a bit too much. I did enjoy the older „event“ system more, because grinding a battle pass is always a commitment and the event skins felt a bit more „thought out“ (some battle pass skins are still solid and the new one looks quite good, but some skins maybe feel slightly lazy, as they just repeat the same design with a few weapons)
The gunplay is still nice, you can still play every gun in the game and at least in my opinion you don’t have to cuckhold yourself with meta gear. Other loadouts are fun too, and every gun (even the deringer) has enough kill potential to be able to do something. The new guns often tend to be stronger at launch, but never unrepairably broken.
My biggest criticism of the game would be the long term progression. While prestigeing does serve that purpose it doesn’t feel too impactful or rewarding, as it is just a number going up. The hunter tier progression was IMO pretty nice, though that system removed some of the cooler looking tier 3 hunter variants, so it would be cool if those could be added back as some form of progression reward or variant too. Other long term goals, that go side by side with the prestige system would be very cool, as that would make the long term incentive to play more stable.
If you‘ve read this far and you have decided to buy the game, maybe we’ll see in the bayou. Have Fun!

So, let me preface this with my current mixed feelings. I'm a Old school Hunt player but I wasn't here from the start, Just like being a Millennial stuck between an dying era and a new era, that's were I sat with hunt for a very long time.

TL;DR: If you never played Hunt and you like large sandboxy experiences in a PvPvE Extraction environment, This is the game for you. If you're an Old head that took a long break from the game, Embrace the changes or stay away as you'll be more heartbroken than anything. Also it's live-service so enjoy it while you can.

Let me lay out the facts before any opinions of mine. Hunt is indeed a Co-op/Solo experience where you interact with other players on a map with objectives. This may be Doing the main objective of Claiming and extracting with any bounty tokens you pick up in a match, or any personal goals a user might set, such as getting their weekly/dailies fulfilled or finding equipment and gear on the map to take back for later deployments. It's a Sandbox experience as Crytek puts it, as you can leave whenever you want, you just need to find the extracts and you can go. 

The Perma death aspect of the game is very minor, if you cannot extract for whatever reason (You died, ran out of time on a map) that hunter is lost, you get a portion of your exp and anything you unlocked during the mission but that's it. It's not a very hardcore experience in that regard as with the way equipment works you'll be back on your feet like nothing happened rather quickly, along with the fact that most of the weapons and tools in the game are very viable to use to kill other players, you just need to be open to using them in a few interesting ways.

The microtransactions have picked up quite a lot but they have done away with the old systems that used to use blood bonds. The only things you can purchase with blood bonds is the current battle pass, bloodline quests, and any skins/hunters/animations off the store you like. You'll always have them so there's no repurchase, you may have to unlock said weapon or item again if you prestige but it will still be yours. Besides that you can still purchase DLC packs if you do not want to purchase the currency if you rather that. Fair warning, you will see hunters/items you don't own or that aren't even available on the store, as it was a limited time event thing before hunt had it's engine upgrade. They are making efforts to bring that content back but it will not be in it's original form entirely, so if that's a pet peeve for you then make a pass on this.

The gameplay is very simple. There's no Shield, No Blue juice or any of that crap. You have 150 HP as a hunter, if you loose it all you get downed and loose one of your big or small bars. If you get headshoted by anything (So long as you take 1 damage to the head excluding pellet based projectiles, melee that's unable to do 150 Damage to the head, and non-weapon tools) you also go down. If you're a solo the only way you can get back up is if you have necromancer, and you lose it once you revive yourself but you get full 150 back no matter what happened.(Unless you already burned your last bar while alive, tough luck.) While if you're in a team, a teammate can pick you back up but you won't recover that bar. Once you're on your last bar if you go down again you're dead for good unless a teammate has a bounty token and gives up some of their bar to pick you up, then you're back on your last one again.

With that all outta the way, let me move on to more opinion based takes.

THE GOOD

Hunt is a great game if you enjoy audio importance, if you love to listen to sounds as each one has important morsels of information to digest to help you win encounters and fights more, or just keep yourself alive from making a foolish choice. Each class of gun has unique sounds, and exotic choices also have another audio cue when close enough so you can already know what kind of fight you're getting into. This does mean it's harder to enjoy the game with noisy company unless you basically silence them but it's very rewarding to make some rather impressive displays of game knowledge just from a few audio cues.

The weapons are very well balanced nowadays, With nothing being an outright winner in all categories. There's no Rifle beats Shotgun, Shotgun beats Pistol kinda archetype here. I can and have won against Snipers or Long rifles with only a Shotgun and melee in tow, but you're pushed to figure out how can you best play with your surroundings and tools to make the best of a bad situation. Everyone is going to have some weaknesses of their loadouts, But playing to their strengths is key to finding yourself walking out with more than you started with.

There are many tools in the game you can use that seemingly have a main purpose but with the interactions in the game world, you'll find out that they can be used in many ways to get the upper hand or cover up a mistake you might have made. I'm not gonna go over all of them but I'll go over the classic Choke bomb in the game. It's a tool you prime and throw like a explosive, but instead of an explosion you get a large blurry choke cloud that will consume any fire within it, and prevent any more fires in it's AoE. If you walk through one, your character will begin to uncontrollably cough, which acts like the aim punch when you take damage. Just with those two facts alone you can create some interesting situations that either buys you some time, or control how your enemies approach you.

THE BAD

You are going to lose, and maybe at best tie with some situations in the game. Doesn't matter if you're solo, duo, or in a trio, sometimes you get into situations where it's practically unwinnable, or you just didn't have enough information to make the right calls in the moment. Because Audio is so key in the game, players will make use of it to draw your attention or avoid it entirely to get the drop on someone, and there's not much you could have done about it but been even more careful.

The kinds of people you'll be encountering in the game is a mixed bag, you'll get a lot of good ones but there's always bad apples in any group. It makes matching up with randoms a bit problematic as you don't know what you're in for if you join up with two other folks that have entirely different goals than you do going into that match. I'm kinda surprised about how much I liked this one. I played a fair bit of Tarkov, but PvE only because PvP stressed me out too much. 

Hunt: Showdown has a pretty solid gameplay loop that lets you play for 30 minutes or 3 hours depending on your mood. Matches are short enough to not be long in the tooth, but long enough to let you get stuck in and actually experience the game. Of course, your raid can be cut short by someone shooting you from 100 meters out, but getting back in is so quick you don't lose much time. 

The old timey guns also gives people who aren't shooter savants a snowball's chance in hell at winning a fight. Positioning is key, and head to head fights aren't as common as you think. Often you'll be shooting at someone who doesn't know you're there, or is otherwise engage with someone else. People will be shooting at you in the same way. The game gives you great feedback about what's going on around you though, so you're never completely clueless. Sounds cues for footsteps, equipment jostling, and gunshots are well defined, and help  quite a bit when deciding tactics in the moment. 

That being said, this game is HARD. You're going to run into a lot of people more experienced than you, and you WILL die more often than not. This game is not for the easily discouraged, and especially not for those who can't find joy in the little victories. 

But if you can swallow your pride and go into this with a student's mindset, there's quite a bit of entertainment to be had.

I started playing Hunt: Showdown right when it left its beta phase, convincing myself to buy it after a friend’s relentless recommendation. I will never forget those first 20-30 matches or the unmatched atmosphere: the "heavy silence" surrounding you, forcing you to listen to every single twig snapping; the pitch-black nights; and the constantly pulsing danger of players and monsters lurking in every shadow. It created an unforgettable, truly unique experience that set it apart from every other FPS on the market. 

Visually, what Crytek created with the CryEngine is nothing short of phenomenal. You get a truly cinematic experience, complemented by a minimal HUD and surprisingly solid performance. Sure, there are occasionally laggier periods especially right after major patches or new map releases but these issues usually get ironed out over time.

Unfortunately, a few persistent bugs have plagued the game for a long time. I consider myself one of the lucky ones with over 500 hours, I’ve only encountered one maybe every 100 hours or so. But when they do happen, they really hurt. In a high-intensity match filled with adrenaline and action, it stings when the game essentially gives you the middle finger and leaves you completely helpless.

It was never an easy game. Even back then, long ammo dominated, and players would gladly rat in bushes for hours. Yet, all of that was easily forgiven because everyone agreed that despite its flaws Hunt was a stroke of genius. A fundamentally fresh concept (I mean, cowboys and zombies? Sounds like a B category film premise, but Hunt made it work flawlessly).

Fast forward a few years, and the game has drifted into a very different direction. Tarot cards, fast-firing weapons, "drone beetles"... Don’t get me wrong, I actually like some of these additions. For example magic was always subtly present, so things like tarot cards fit the lore and can be interesting mechanic. But somewhere along the way, the core soul felt a bit lost. Matches feel increasingly rushed and shifted away from hunting bosses or engaging in meaningful PvP to grinding through Battle Passes and getting rare skins.

At its core, Hunt is still a brilliant, pioneering diamond in the rough. However, sometimes less is more IMO. Many of the mechanics and additions bloat the experience rather than genuinely improve it. I deeply miss the simplicity that once defined it (WHICH already came with a CRAZY steep learning curve).

I don't necessarily blame the developers... it's a live-service game, and they have to sustain a business model. And it remains a deeply enjoyable game, BUT I think, it has been heading in the wrong direction for quite a while now.
If you thinking of getting the game, at least do so on a sale, see if it clicks with you. Happy Hunting!!

⭐ Hunt: Showdown — A Brutal, Beautiful, Beginner‑Friendly Extraction Shooter
Hunt: Showdown is one of those rare extraction shooters that feels intimidating at first glance but becomes incredibly rewarding once you step inside its world. What makes it stand out is how welcoming it actually is for beginners. The game teaches you to slow down, listen, and think — and once you get the rhythm, Hunt becomes one of the most addictive shooters out there.

A Diverse Cast That Actually Feels Meaningful
One thing I’ve always loved about Hunt is how diverse its roster of Hunters is. Crytek doesn’t just throw in random characters — they build personalities, backgrounds, and visual identities that make the world feel alive. You see representation across different ethnicities, genders, and styles, and it never feels forced. It feels like a world full of real people who ended up in the bayou fighting monsters.

Beginner-Friendly Despite Its Reputation
People love to say Hunt is “hard,” but honestly, it’s one of the easiest extraction shooters to get into once you understand the basics. Unlike other extraction games that drown you in loot systems, armor tiers, and endless menus, Hunt keeps it simple:

You pick a Hunter

You pick your weapons

You go into the bayou

You survive

The clarity of the design makes it way easier for new players to learn positioning, sound awareness, and pacing. And once you get your first few kills, the game hooks you forever.

DLC That Gives Real Variety
Hunt’s DLC packs are some of the best in the genre because they actually give you variety, not just recolors. New Hunters come with unique vibes, new weapon skins feel fresh, and the cosmetics help you express your identity in-game. Whether you want something gritty, stylish, creepy, or heroic, Hunt’s DLC lineup has something for every playstyle and personality.

Giggle the Clown — One of My Favorites
Giggle the Clown is easily one of the most iconic Hunters in the entire game. The design is creepy, funny, and stylish all at once — and running around the bayou as Giggle feels like you’re starring in your own horror movie. The in‑game store makes it easy to grab characters like Giggle without any grind or nonsense, and it’s one of the reasons I love Hunt’s cosmetic system.

Necromancer — A Solo Player’s Best Friend
If you play solo, Necromancer is one of the strongest abilities in the game. Being able to revive yourself changes everything:

You can take more risks

You can clutch fights you “should’ve lost”

You can outplay duos and trios

You stay in the match longer instead of instantly dying

Necromancer gives solo players a fighting chance, and it’s one of the reasons Hunt feels fair even when you’re outnumbered.

Final Thoughts
Hunt: Showdown is a masterpiece of atmosphere, tension, and tactical gunplay. It’s diverse, beginner‑friendly, and full of personality thanks to its DLC lineup and unforgettable Hunters like Giggle the Clown. And if you’re a solo player, Necromancer turns the game into a whole new experience.

It’s one of the most unique shooters ever made — and it deserves way more players.

This game appeared on my radar not long ago, but it has already become one of my favorites. PvE, PvP, zombies, and realistic gunplay  are things I don't see combined this well in modern games. Its Worth A Try Guys!

What I really like about this game is that every move has to be considered. You can't just run around and start shooting everyone you see. You have to stay alert and listen carefully to every sound  gunshots, footsteps, animals, and even the environment itself. The jungle feels truly alive, and even the slightest sound can give away your position.

The game has that Red Dead Redemption 2 old-school gun feeling, combined with zombies and intense PvP. The graphics are also absolutely breathtaking, especially considering how atmospheric and immersive the maps are.

It can definitely be difficult for new players at first, but once you start understanding the weapons, sound cues, movement, and PvP encounters, the game becomes incredibly fun and rewarding.

I also really love the fact that it doesn't feel pay-to-win. You can earn Blood Bonds by playing the game, while also having the option to purchase them. The items you can buy don't ruin the competitive aspect of the game, which I really appreciate.

After only 10 hours of playing, I'm confident enough to give this game a 10/10. I got it on sale, and honestly, it was worth every penny.

It might not be the most popular game out there, but if you're looking for a combination of RDR2 + zombies + PvP + realism, I definitely recommend giving Hunt: Showdown a try.

And yeah, having your own team makes the game even better. 😂

I'll update this review in the future if my opinion changes or I discover anything new.

I’d just like the option to enjoy the gameplay, explore the mechanics, fight AI enemies, and spend more time in the game without always having to participate in PvP.

The primary focus of this game is fighting bosses/getting bounty tokens and pvp. Hunt: Showdown 1896 is one of the most intense and unique shooters I’ve ever played. What makes it stand out is the way it combines PvP, PvE, survival, and extraction into one experience. Every match feels dangerous because you’re not only fighting monsters—you’re also listening for other Hunters who could be waiting around the next corner. The sound design is especially incredible; a single gunshot, broken window, or set of footsteps can completely change the way you approach a fight

The gunplay is slower and more deliberate than in most modern shooters, which makes every shot feel important. You have to think about your positioning, ammunition, noise, and when it’s actually worth taking a fight. The bounty system makes things even more exciting because once you claim the bounty, you become a target for everyone else, turning the trip to extraction into one of the most stressful parts of the match.

The atmosphere is another huge strength. The dark western setting, creepy monsters, abandoned locations, weather, and incredible audio create an atmosphere that very few multiplayer games can match. The game can be terrifying even when nothing is happening, because you never know when another Hunter is going to appear.

Overall, I’d give Hunt: Showdown 1896 a 9/10. It can be frustrating, unforgiving, and difficult to learn, but that’s also what makes winning feel so rewarding. When you survive a fight, grab the bounty, and successfully extract while knowing another team was hunting you, there’s genuinely nothing quite like it.

[h1]One of the best games ever[/h1]

Hunt: Showdown has one of the steepest learning curves I have ever experienced in a video game.

The good thing is: [b]you start making progress surprisingly soon.[/b]

The better thing is: [b]you never really stop learning.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]You will lose. A lot.[/h2]

You will lose hunters, equipment, money, and sometimes fights where you still have no idea what just happened.

Modern games often try very hard to keep players comfortable and make sure you never really lose anything important.

[b]Hunt is different.[/b]

It can be hard. It can be frustrating. Sometimes you will have a terrible day and lose hunter after hunter.

But that's exactly why every victory feels so damn good.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The atmosphere. The sound. The details.[/h2]

The atmosphere is among the best I have ever experienced in a video game.

[i]Maybe the best.[/i]

And the sound? [b]Absolutely incredible.[/b]

I highly recommend playing with good stereo headphones. With Crytek's own sound engine, sound is not just there to make the game feel immersive — it is an essential part of how you understand and play the game.

Every match feels special.

I still remember great plays and intense moments from [b]2024[/b]. How many games can you say that about?

The attention to detail is insane.

The weapons. The reload mechanics. The different animations.

And the weapon sounds...

[b]Oh my god, the weapon sounds.[/b]

I don't even care about weapons in real life. But in Hunt?

[i]That's something completely different.[/i]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]And then everything comes together.[/h2]

The most rewarding moments are when everything you have learned suddenly pays off.

You hear something.

You notice a clue.

You understand what is happening somewhere on the map.

You make a prediction.

And then...

[b]You are right.[/b]

You make the right decision because you understood the situation — and that decision wins you the match.

[quote]Yeah. That's Hunt.[/quote]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]But some days, Hunt is also just losing.[/h2]

[b]A lot.[/b]

And honestly?

[i]That's okay.[/i]

It's not always about winning the round.

Sometimes it's about the journey.

About learning something new.

About having an incredible fight, even if you lose in the end.

And even after a bad match, you might have unlocked something new for your inventory.

Then you buy another hunter.

You equip your weapons.

You enter the bayou.

And somehow...

[b][h2]You just can't wait to do it all again - See you in the Bayou[/h2][/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]A small technical note[/h2]

I recommend experimenting with your DLSS and sharpening settings.

Using an aggressive DLSS setting without enough sharpening can make the game look a bit washed out, especially in certain weather conditions or at night.

It's not necessarily a problem with the game's art style — the right balance between DLSS and sharpening can make a noticeable difference.

Unique game mechanics in a visually impressive Southern Gothic setting. PvE and PvP are both engaging and with lots of creative opportunities to take advantage of the interactive environments and player-placed traps. Nice assortment of weapons and equipment to customize the way you play, not hidden behind a painful grind either so even new players stand a fighting chance. The cosmetic customization fits in with the supernatural setting and doesn't stick out like a sore thumb. The detailed environments, sound design, tension and atmosphere are what really makes this game stand out. A hardcore game with a slow and deliberate pace where every moment could be your last. You need to carefully consider how you traverse the environment and approach compounds, stick to cover and avoid making unneccessary sound. No place for running and gunning. You might get sniped in the open out of the blue occassionally, but a general lack of long sightlines and compact map design means most firefights take place in close quarters leading to Wild West-style shootouts where careful aim and managing your limited ammo and long reloads is essential. Most of the time you hear hostile hunters before you see them which gives you tactical options in how and when to engage or to avoid confrontation altogether. The tempo in which matches unfold makes them engaging from start to finish and there are multiple ways to approach your objectives, earn rewards and extract successfully if you are patient and plan ahead.
